proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(\eta\) denote the true nuisance triple and set
\(\phi(\bar\eta;O)=\psi_1(\bar\eta;O)-\psi_0(\bar\eta;O)\).  The definitions give the exact identity
\[
 \phi(\eta;O)=\theta+D(O). \tag{20}
\]
We first establish the continuity needed for cross-fitting.  If the three uniform primitive errors of an in-band triple are at most \(e\), then
\[
 |\bar H_a(t,x)-H_a(t,x)|
 \le\int_t^1\int_t^v|\bar\lambda_a(s,x)-\lambda_a(s,x)|\,ds\,dv
 \le\tfrac12e(1-t)^2. \tag{21}
\]
Using the propensity and residual lower bounds in (21) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\bar H_a}{\bar G_a}-\frac{H_a}{G_a}\right|
 +\left|\frac{\bar H_a\bar\lambda_a}{\bar G_a}-
 \frac{H_a\lambda_a}{G_a}\right|
 \le \frac{Ce}{1-t},
 \qquad |\bar m_a-m_a|\le Ce. \tag{22}
\]
The same calculation includes the change of \(1/\bar\pi_a\).  With the envelope \(B\) from (17), it follows that
\[
 |\phi(\bar\eta;O)-\phi(\eta;O)|\le CeB(O),
 \qquad E_P\{\phi(\bar\eta;O)-\phi(\eta;O)\}^2\le Ce^2, \tag{23}
\]
uniformly over the class.  Because every fitted primitive is clipped to its primitive band, the first bound with \(e\) replaced by a class constant also holds off the nuisance good event.

Let \(\mathcal G_k\) be the event that the learner trained off fold \(k\) has total uniform error at most \(Cr_M\), where its training size differs from \(n/2\) by at most one.  The resolved primitive concentration theorem and the rate calculation there imply
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P(\mathcal G_k^c)\to0,
 \qquad r_M=O\{(\log n/n)^{1/3}\}. \tag{24}
\]
On \(\mathcal G_k\), lem:exact-integrated-drift applied armwise gives
\[
 |E_P\{\phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O)\mid\widehat\eta_{-k}\}-\theta|
 \le Cr_M^2. \tag{25}
\]
Conditional on its opposite-fold training data, the observations in validation fold \(k\) are independent of \(\widehat\eta_{-k}\).  By (23), the conditional variance of
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i:k(i)=k}
 \left[\phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O_i)-\phi(\eta;O_i)
 -E_P\{\phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O)-\phi(\eta;O)\mid\widehat\eta_{-k}\}\right]
\]
is at most \(Cr_M^2\).  Conditional Chebyshev inequality, (24), and a union bound over the two folds make this expression \(o_P(1)\), uniformly in \(P\).  The conditional means contribute at most
\[
 C\sqrt n,r_M^2=O\{n^{-1/6}(\log n)^{2/3}\}=o(1) \tag{26}
\]
by (25).  Equations (20)--(26) prove the first asserted uniform expansion.

For variance estimation, choose once and for all \(p=5/2\).  Lem:endpoint-moment-envelope gives \(\sup_PE_P|D|^p<\infty\).  Consequently, uniformly in \(P\),
\[
 E_P[D^2\mathbf1\{|D|>K\}]\le K^{2-p}E_P|D|^p\longrightarrow0
 \quad(K\to\infty). \tag{27}
\]
For fixed \(K\), Chebyshev's inequality applies to the bounded truncation of \(D^2\); (27), first taking \(n\to\infty\) and then \(K\to\infty\), proves
\[
 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)^2-E_PD(O)^2=o_P(1) \tag{28}
\]
uniformly.  The analogous, easier truncation proves \(n^{-1}\sum_iD(O_i)=o_P(1)\) uniformly.

By (23), conditional Markov inequality on each good training event shows
\[
 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\{W_i-\theta-D(O_i)\}^2=o_P(1) \tag{29}
\]
uniformly; (24) removes the bad events.  Cauchy--Schwarz, (28), and (29) imply that the empirical centered second moment of the \(W_i\)'s differs from that of the \(D(O_i)\)'s by \(o_P(1)\).  Thus it converges uniformly to \(V_P\).  By lem:endpoint-moment-envelope, \(V_P\ge c>0\), so the floor \(n^{-1}\) is inactive with probability tending uniformly to one and
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P\{|\widehat V/V_P-1|>\varepsilon\}\to0. \tag{30}
\]

It remains to justify the uniform normal approximation without a third moment.  Put \(Z_P=D/\sqrt{V_P}\).  Then \(E_PZ_P=0\), \(E_PZ_P^2=1\), and, for \(p=5/2\),
\(\sup_PE_P|Z_P|^p<\infty\).  For any sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_4\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 E_{P_n}\{Z_{P_n}^2\mathbf1(|Z_{P_n}|>\varepsilon\sqrt n)\}
 \le C(\varepsilon\sqrt n)^{2-p}\to0. \tag{31}
\]
The elementary characteristic-function proof of the Lindeberg theorem applies: Taylor-expand
\(e^{itZ_{P_n}/\sqrt n}\) on \(|Z_{P_n}|\le\varepsilon\sqrt n\), bound the complement by (31), let \(n\to\infty\), and then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).  It gives
\[
 \left(E_{P_n}e^{itZ_{P_n}/\sqrt n}\right)^n\to e^{-t^2/2}
\]
for each real \(t\).  Hence the normalized sum converges weakly to a standard normal along every sequence \(P_n\).  Continuity of \(\Phi\) upgrades this to Kolmogorov convergence.  If the convergence were not uniform in \(P\), a violating sequence \(P_n\) would contradict this argument; therefore
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}\sup_z
 \left|P\!\left\{n^{-1/2}\sum_iD(O_i)/\sqrt{V_P}\le z\right\}-\Phi(z)\right|\to0. \tag{32}
\]
Finally, the first expansion divided by the uniform positive lower bound for \(\sqrt{V_P}\), together with (30), implies that the studentized statistic differs uniformly in probability from the variable in (32).  Uniform tightness and the uniform continuity of \(\Phi\) give the stated uniform Slutsky conclusion.  Every fitting operation used here is the total measurable completion in the resolved concentration theorem and uses only the sample and fixed class constants.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\).  Identification, which is given in the setup, writes the observed-law functional as
\[
 \theta(P)=E_P\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)\}. \tag{33}
\]
By lem:endpoint-moment-envelope, \(D\in L_0^2(P)\).  Consider a regular dominated one-dimensional submodel through \(P\).  The independent-censoring likelihood factorization decomposes its score orthogonally into a covariate score \(s_X(X)\) with \(E_Ps_X=0\), a treatment score with conditional mean zero given \(X\), event-martingale scores, and censoring-martingale scores.  It suffices to verify the derivative on each component.

For the covariate component, differentiating (33) gives
\[
 \dot\theta_X=E_P[\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)-\theta\}s_X(X)]. \tag{34}
\]
The conditional martingale means in the definition of \(D\) vanish, so the right side of (34) is \(E_P[Ds_X]\).  Treatment perturbations leave (33) fixed.  Their scores have conditional mean zero given \(X\), and the event terms have conditional mean zero given \((A,X)\); hence their covariance with \(D\) is zero.

For an event-hazard log-direction \(b_a(t,x)\), smooth, bounded, and supported in \(t\le1-\epsilon\), use
\(\lambda_{a,\varepsilon}=\lambda_a\exp(\varepsilon b_a)\).  Differentiation under the bounded survival integral and Fubini give
\[
 \dot\theta_a(b_a)
 =-E_P\!\left[\int_0^1S_a(t\mid X)H_a(t,X)\lambda_a(t,X)b_a(t,X)\,dt\right]. \tag{35}
\]
The corresponding observed-data score is
\(\mathbf1\{A=a\}\int b_a(t,X)\,dM_a(t)\).  Let \(\sigma_1=1\) and \(\sigma_0=-1\).  Martingale isometry and conditional independent censoring yield
\[
 E_P\!\left[D\,\mathbf1\{A=a\}\int b_a\,dM_a\right]
 =-\sigma_aE_P\!\left[\int_0^1S_aH_a\lambda_ab_a\,dt\right]
 =\dot\theta(b_a), \tag{36}
\]
which is the derivative of the contrast.  A censoring-hazard score is a stochastic integral with respect to the censoring martingale.  It is orthogonal to the event martingale because there are no simultaneous event and censoring jumps before one, and it is orthogonal to the covariate term by conditional mean zero.  Since (33) does not depend on the censoring law, both its derivative and its covariance with \(D\) are zero.  Thus (34)--(36) prove that \(D\) represents the pathwise derivative for every regular score.

We next show that this representer is in the relevant tangent closure despite the endpoint singularity.  The event-information measure for arm \(a\) is
\[
 d\mu_a(t,x)=f(x)\pi_a(x)S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x)\lambda_a(t,x)\,dt\,dx.
\]
The event coefficient \(H_a/(\pi_aG_a)\) belongs to \(L^2(\mu_a)\) by (15).  From the primitive bands and (14), the squared \(L^2(\mu_a)\) norm discarded on \((1-\epsilon,1)\) is at most
\[
 C\int_{1-\epsilon}^1\frac{H_a(t,x)^2}{G_a(t\mid x)}\,dt\,dx\le C\epsilon. \tag{37}
\]
After truncation below \(1-\epsilon\), bounded smooth functions are dense in this weighted \(L^2\) space because its density is bounded above and below on compact subrectangles.  The interior slack in the hazard bands and Hölder radius makes each sufficiently small two-sided smooth compactly supported log-hazard perturbation admissible.  Therefore the event part of \(D\) is in the closure of admissible smooth event scores.  The covariate part belongs to the covariate tangent closure: bounded mean-zero perturbations of \(f\) are admissible under the essential interior density slack, and smooth bounded functions are dense in \(L^2(f)\).  Consequently \(D\) itself lies in the tangent closure.  Its squared norm is, by definition and (15), \(E_PD^2=V_P\).

The preceding covariance identities and closure establish that \(D\) is the canonical gradient.  Lem:semiparametric-convolution-bound now implies that every regular estimator has asymptotic variance at least \(V_P\).  Finally, thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency gives at this fixed \(P\)
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)+o_P(1),
\]
and the central limit argument in its proof gives limit \(N(0,V_P)\).  Along every fixed smooth local submodel through this interior law, its \(n^{-1/2}\)-local members remain in \(\mathcal P_4\); continuity of the displayed nuisance functions implies \(D_{P_n}\to D_P\) in \(L^2\).  The uniform expansion therefore gives the same centered \(N(0,V_P)\) limit along those local alternatives, which is regularity and attainment of the bound.

Fix an arm \(a\), a law \(P\in\mathcal P_4\), and an in-band deterministic triple \(\bar\eta\).  Conditional independent censoring and the no-atom condition give
\[
 E_P\{Y_{\mathrm{risk}}(t)\mid A=a,X=x\}=S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x),
\]
and
\[
 P\{U\in dt,\Delta=1\mid A=a,X=x\}
 =S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x)\lambda_a(t,x)\,dt.
\]
All ensuing integrals are absolutely integrable: \(\bar H_a(t,x)\le1-t\), \(G_a/\bar G_a=g_a/\bar g_a\le4\), and both hazards are bounded.  Tonelli and Fubini are therefore applicable.  The conditional mean of the expression in braces in def:rmst-score equals
\[
 \int_0^1 S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x)
 \frac{\bar H_a(t,x)}{\bar G_a(t\mid x)}
 \{\lambda_a(t,x)-\bar\lambda_a(t,x)\}\,dt. \tag{12}
\]
For \(v\in[0,1]\), differentiation along the segment
\(\lambda_{a,s}=\lambda_a+s(\bar\lambda_a-\lambda_a)\) and integration in \(s\) give the Duhamel identity
\[
 \bar S_a(v\mid x)-S_a(v\mid x)
 =-\int_0^v S_a(t\mid x)\bar S_a(v\mid x)\bar S_a(t\mid x)^{-1}
 \{\bar\lambda_a(t,x)-\lambda_a(t,x)\}\,dt.
\]
Integration in \(v\), followed by Fubini, yields
\[
 \bar m_a(x)-m_a(x)
 =-\int_0^1S_a(t\mid x)\bar H_a(t,x)
 \{\bar\lambda_a(t,x)-\lambda_a(t,x)\}\,dt. \tag{13}
\]
Multiply (12) by the conditional treatment probability \(\pi_a(x)\), by the score factor \(-1/\bar\pi_a(x)\), and add (13).  Since
\(G_a/\bar G_a=g_a/\bar g_a\) for every \(t<1\), we obtain pointwise in \(x\), and hence after averaging over \(X\),
\[
 E_P[\psi_a(\bar\eta;O)]-\theta_a
 =E_P\!\left[\int_0^1S_a(t\mid X)\bar H_a(t,X)
 \left\{\frac{\pi_a(X)g_a(t,X)}{\bar\pi_a(X)\bar g_a(t,X)}-1\right\}
 \{\bar\lambda_a(t,X)-\lambda_a(t,X)\}\,dt\right].
\]
The denominator in the ratio is at least \((1/4)(1/2)=1/8\), whereas
\[
 |\pi_ag_a-\bar\pi_a\bar g_a|
 \le |\pi_a|\,|g_a-\bar g_a|+|\bar g_a|\,|\pi_a-\bar\pi_a|
 \le \lVert g_a-\bar g_a\rVert_\infty+2\lVert\pi_a-\bar\pi_a\rVert_\infty.
\]
Together with \(S_a\le1\), \(\bar H_a(t,x)\le1-t\), and integration over a unit interval, this proves the asserted product bound with a class constant.

Write \(r=1-t\).  The hazard band implies, uniformly in \((a,t,x)\),
\[
 e^{-2}\le S_a(t\mid x)\le1,
 \qquad e^{-2}r\le H_a(t,x)=\int_t^1
 \exp\!\left\{-\int_t^v\lambda_a(s,x)\,ds\right\}dv\le r. \tag{14}
\]
The one-jump martingale isometry, justified directly from the two conditional relations in the proof of lem:exact-integrated-drift, gives
\[
 V_P=\operatorname{Var}_P\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)\}
 +E_P\!\left[\sum_{a=0}^1\frac1{\pi_a(X)}
 \int_0^1\frac{H_a(t,X)^2S_a(t\mid X)\lambda_a(t,X)}{G_a(t\mid X)}\,dt\right]. \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, the two arm martingales are orthogonal because their treatment indicators are disjoint, and each has conditional mean zero given \(X\), so both are orthogonal to the covariate term.  By (14), \(G_a=r^2g_a\), and the primitive bands, each integrand in (15) is at least \(e^{-6}/4\).  Since
\(1/\pi_0+1/\pi_1\ge4\),
\[
 V_P\ge e^{-6}. \tag{16}
\]
The same relations bound each integrand by \(4\), while \(1/\pi_a\le4\), and the covariate contrast lies in \([-1,1]\); thus, for example, \(V_P\le33\).  This establishes the two uniform variance bounds.

The score itself obeys a sharper observationwise envelope.  From (14), \(G_a\ge r^2/2\), \(\lambda_a\le2\), and \(1/\pi_a\le4\),
\[
 |D(O)|\le C\left[1+\frac{\Delta}{1-U}
 +\log\!\left\{\frac1{1-U}\right\}\right]=:C B(O). \tag{17}
\]
Conditionally on \((A=a,X=x)\), the observed-event density is bounded above by
\(4(1-t)^2\).  Hence, for \(2<p<3\),
\[
 E_P\!\left[\frac{\Delta}{(1-U)^p}\,middle|,A=a,X=x\right]
 \le4\int_0^1r^{2-p}\,dr=\frac4{3-p}. \tag{18}
\]
Also, by conditional independent censoring,
\[
 P\!\left\{\log\frac1{1-U}>v\,middle|,A=a,X=x\right\}
 =P\{U>1-e^{-v}\mid A=a,X=x\}
 \le2e^{-2v}. \tag{19}
\]
The tail-integral formula applied to (19) gives every positive moment of the logarithm uniformly.  Equations (17)--(19) and \((x+y+z)^p\le3^{p-1}(x^p+y^p+z^p)\) prove
\(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}E_P|D(O)|^p<\infty\) for every fixed \(p\in(2,3)\).

Under \(P^{\star}\), the density is \(f\equiv1\), the propensity ranges from \(0.4\) to \(0.6\), the two hazards range within \([1,1.75]\), and
\(g_a(t,x)=e^{-xt/4}\in[e^{-1/4},1]\).  The derivatives through order three and the Lipschitz constants of the third derivatives of these functions are all strictly smaller than \(20\).  Every displayed band and Hölder-radius constraint consequently has positive slack.  Moreover,
\[
 \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\{(1-t)^2e^{-xt/4}\}
 =-e^{-xt/4}\left\{2(1-t)+\frac{x}{4}(1-t)^2\right\}\le0,
\]
the survival starts at one and decreases continuously to zero, and the stated conditional construction supplies consistency, treatment exchangeability, and independent censoring.  Hence \(P^{\star}\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\).

The \(5/2\)-moment assertion follows immediately from lem:endpoint-moment-envelope.  To prove that the third moment is infinite, fix either arm and write \(r=1-t\).  The bands, or the explicit exponential formula, give constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) such that for all sufficiently small \(r\),
\[
 \frac{H_a(1-r,x)}{G_a(1-r\mid x)}\ge\frac{c_1}{r},
 \qquad
 \int_0^{1-r}\frac{H_a(t,x)\lambda_a(t,x)}{G_a(t\mid x)}\,dt
 \le c_2\log(1/r). \tag{38}
\]
On \(A=a\) and an observed event at \(U=1-r\), the event jump in the corresponding arm component of \(D\) has absolute size at least \(c_1/(\pi_a(X)r)\), whereas all remaining terms are bounded by a constant plus \(c_2\log(1/r)\).  Thus, for some \(r_0,c_3>0\), \(|D|\ge c_3/r\) on such events with \(r<r_0\).  Their conditional density is
\[
 S_a(1-r\mid x)G_a(1-r\mid x)\lambda_a(1-r,x)\,dr\ge c_4r^2\,dr
\]
for a constant \(c_4>0\).  Treatment probabilities are uniformly positive, so Tonelli's theorem and (38) yield
\[
 E_{P^{\star}}|D(O)|^3
 \ge c_5\int_0^{r_0}r^{-3}r^2\,dr
 =\infty.
\]
This proves both moment claims without invoking a third- or fourth-moment bound.

By def:wald-interval,
\[
 \{\theta\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}
 =\left\{\left|\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)}{\sqrt{\widehat V}}\right|
 \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\right\}.
\]
The uniform Kolmogorov convergence in thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency applies at both fixed continuity points \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) and \(-z_{1-\alpha/2}\).  Since a standard normal distribution assigns no mass to either endpoint,
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}\left|
 P\{\theta\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}
 -\{\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2})-\Phi(-z_{1-\alpha/2})\}\right|\to0.
\]
By the definition of the quantile and symmetry of \(\Phi\), the expression in braces equals \(1-\alpha\), proving the proposition.

theorem.statement:
The answer is affirmative.  The local-cubic handle in def:endpoint-learning-handle has a measurable total completion for which there are constants \(C,c>0\), depending only on the displayed class constants and the fixed polynomial bases, such that for all sufficiently large \(M\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P\!\left(
 \max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\lVert\widehat\lambda_a-\lambda_a\rVert_\infty+
 \max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\lVert\widehat g_a-g_a\rVert_\infty+
 \lVert\widehat\pi_1-\pi_1\rVert_\infty>C r_M\right)
 \le C M^{-2}+C J_M^2\exp(-cMh_M^3).
\]
In particular, \(r_M=O\{(\log M/M)^{1/3}\}\), uniformly over the arbitrary measurable covariate densities allowed by \(\mathcal P_4\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Put \(J=J_M\), \(h=h_M\), \(I_j=[jh,(j+1)h)\), \(K_\ell=[\ell h,(\ell+1)h)\), and \(d_j=1-jh\), with the usual inclusion of the right endpoint in the last covariate cell.  Let \(p(z_t,z_x)\) be the vector of the ten monomials of total degree at most three and let \(L:=\sup_{[0,1]^2}\lVert p\rVert<\infty\).  Define
\[
 B_*:=\int_{[0,1]^2}(1-z_t)^2p(z_t,z_x)p(z_t,z_x)^{\mathsf T}\,dz_t\,dz_x,
 \qquad \beta_*:=\lambda_{\min}(B_*).
\]
For every nonzero vector \(u\), the polynomial \(u^{\mathsf T}p\) is nonzero on an open subset, so \(u^{\mathsf T}B_*u>0\); hence \(\beta_*>0\).  This number and all thresholds below are fixed class-known constants.

We first record the elementary concentration inequality used throughout.  If independent centered variables \(Z_i\) obey \(|Z_i|\le b\) and \(\sum_iE Z_i^2\le v\), expansion of the exponential series and \(k!\ge2\,3^{k-2}\) for \(k\ge2\) gives, for \(0<s<3/b\),
\[
 \log E\exp\!\left(s\sum_iZ_i\right)
 \le \frac{s^2v}{2(1-sb/3)}.
\]
Exponential Markov inequality, optimized at \(s=u/(v+bu/3)\), and the same argument for \(-Z_i\), therefore give
\[
 P\!\left(\left|\sum_iZ_i\right|>u\right)
 \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{u^2}{2(v+bu/3)}\right\}. \tag{1}
\]
Thus no concentration property is being added to the model.

For arm \(a\) and cell \((j,\ell)\), complete the hazard part of the handle by
\[
 R_{aj\ell}:=\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}
 \int_{I_j}Y_{i,\mathrm{risk}}(t)p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)^{\mathsf T}\,dt,
\]
\[
 b_{aj\ell}:=\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell,U_i\in I_j,\Delta_i=1\}
 p_{j\ell}(U_i,X_i),
\]
where \(p_{j\ell}(t,x)=p((t-jh)/h,(x-\ell h)/h)\).  Conditional independent censoring and the absence of atoms before one imply
\[
 E_P\{Y_{\mathrm{risk}}(t)\mid A=a,X=x\}=S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x),
\quad
 P\{U\in dt,\Delta=1\mid A=a,X=x\}=S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x)\lambda_a(t,x)\,dt. \tag{2}
\]
The density, overlap, survival, and residual bands give
\[
 f(x)\pi_a(x)S_a(t\mid x)g_a(t,x)\ge e^{-2}/16.
\]
Since \(1-t=d_j-hz_t\ge d_j(1-z_t)\), change of variables in the population Gram matrix yields
\[
 \lambda_{\min}\{E_PR_{aj\ell}\}
 \ge (e^{-2}\beta_*/16)Mh^2d_j^2. \tag{3}
\]
An entry of one summand of \(R_{aj\ell}\) is bounded by \(L^2h\).  By Cauchy--Schwarz, (2), and the upper primitive bands, its variance is at most \(C h^3d_j^2\).  Apply (1) to the fixed number of entries and use \(\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le10\max_{r,s}|B_{rs}|\).  Weyl's inequality and (3) then show
\[
 P\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}(R_{aj\ell})<e^{-2}\beta_*Mh^2d_j^2/32\right\}
 \le C\exp(-cMhd_j^2)\le C\exp(-cMh^3). \tag{4}
\]
The same event also bounds the trace, and hence the total cell exposure, by \(CMh^2d_j^2\).

Let \(\lambda^0_{aj\ell}=p_{j\ell}^{\mathsf T}\gamma^0_{aj\ell}\) be the third-order Taylor polynomial of \(\lambda_a\) at the lower-left cell corner, interpreted one-sidedly on boundary cells.  The radius-
\(20\) \(C^{3,1}\) condition and the multivariate Taylor formula give
\[
 \sup_{I_j\times K_\ell}|\lambda_a-\lambda^0_{aj\ell}|\le C h^4. \tag{5}
\]
The exact normal-equation decomposition is
\[
 b_{aj\ell}-R_{aj\ell}\gamma^0_{aj\ell}
 =\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}
 \int_{I_j}p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)\,dM_{a,i}(t)
 +\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}
 \int_{I_j}Y_{i,\mathrm{risk}}(t)p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)
 \{\lambda_a(t,X_i)-\lambda^0_{aj\ell}(t,X_i)\}\,dt. \tag{6}
\]
For each coordinate, the first summand over a subject is centered by (2), is bounded by a class constant, and has variance at most \(C h^2d_j^2\).  The variance identity follows directly by expanding the one-jump expression in (6), using the two relations in (2), and applying Fubini; it is the usual one-jump martingale isometry.  Taking \(u=C\{(Mh^2d_j^2\log(M+2))^{1/2}+\log(M+2)\}\) in (1), and taking the constant large enough, gives failure probability at most \(CM^{-5}\) for every coordinate.  On the Gram event, (5), (6), the exposure bound following (4), and inversion of (3) give
\[
 \sup_{I_j\times K_\ell}|\widehat\lambda_a-\lambda_a|
 \le C\left[h^4+sqrt{\frac{\log(M+2)}{Mh^2d_j^2}}+
 \frac{\log(M+2)}{Mh^2d_j^2}\right]. \tag{7}
\]
Pointwise clipping cannot increase the error because the true hazard lies in the clipping interval.  Since \(d_j\ge h\), the right side of (7) is at most \(Cr_M\).

We next complete the rescaled-risk fit.  Set
\[
 Q_{aj\ell}:=\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}
 \int_{I_j}(1-t)^2p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)^{\mathsf T}\,dt,
\]
\[
 c_{aj\ell}:=\sum_{i=1}^M\mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}
 \int_{I_j}Y_{i,\mathrm{risk}}(t)p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)\,dt.
\]
Now \(f\pi_a\ge1/8\), whence
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(E_PQ_{aj\ell})\ge(\beta_*/8)Mh^2d_j^2. \tag{8}
\]
An entry of a summand is bounded by \(Chd_j^2\) and has variance at most \(Ch^3d_j^4\).  The argument leading to (4) gives a Gram failure probability at most \(C\exp(-cMh)\).  The function \(q_a=S_ag_a\) has a class-uniform \(C^{3,1}\) norm: this follows successively from differentiation under the integral defining \(S_a\), the product and chain rules, the hazard band, and the two radius-
\(20\) Hölder bounds.  Its cellwise cubic Taylor error is consequently at most \(Ch^4\).

The centered coordinate of the response normal equation is
\[
 \mathbf1\{A_i=a,X_i\in K_\ell\}\int_{I_j}p_{j\ell}(t,X_i)
 \{Y_{i,\mathrm{risk}}(t)-(1-t)^2q_a(t,X_i)\}\,dt.
\]
It is bounded by \(Ch\).  From (2) and Cauchy--Schwarz its variance is at most \(Ch^3d_j^2\).  Applying (1), (8), and the Taylor bound therefore yields, simultaneously on the cell,
\[
 \lVert\widehat q_a^{\mathrm{raw}}-q_a\rVert_\infty
 \le C\left[h^4+sqrt{\frac{\log(M+2)}{Mhd_j^2}}+
 \frac{\log(M+2)}{Mhd_j^2}\right]
 \le Cr_M. \tag{9}
\]
The hazard band gives \(e^{-2}\le S_a,\widehat S_a\le1\), and the exponential map gives
\[
 \lVert\widehat S_a-S_a\rVert_\infty
 \le\lVert\widehat\lambda_a-\lambda_a\rVert_\infty.
\]
Because \(q_a=S_ag_a\), division by \(\widehat S_a\), followed by clipping to \([1/2,2]\), transforms (7)--(9) into
\[
 \lVert\widehat g_a-g_a\rVert_\infty\le Cr_M. \tag{10}
\]

Finally, on every \(K_\ell\), regress \(A\) on the four normalized monomials of degrees zero through three.  The population Gram has minimum eigenvalue at least \(Mh\beta_\pi/2\), where \(\beta_\pi>0\) is the smallest eigenvalue of \(\int_0^1v(z)v(z)^{\mathsf T}dz\).  Entrywise use of (1) gives Gram failure probability \(C\exp(-cMh)\).  Taylor expansion of \(\pi_1\), and (1) applied to \(\mathbf1\{X_i\in K_\ell\}v(X_i)\{A_i-\pi_1(X_i)\}\), give
\[
 \lVert\widehat\pi_1-\pi_1\rVert_\infty
 \le C\left[h^4+\sqrt{\frac{\log(M+2)}{Mh}}+
 \frac{\log(M+2)}{Mh}\right]\le Cr_M. \tag{11}
\]
Again clipping is nonexpansive relative to the true in-band function.

There are two arms, \(J^2\) time--covariate cells, and \(J\) propensity cells, while all matrix dimensions are fixed.  A union bound over (4) and its \(Q\)- and propensity analogues contributes at most \(CJ^2e^{-cMh^3}\).  Choosing the constants in the numerator thresholds so that their union contributes at most \(CM^{-2}\), equations (7), (10), and (11) prove the displayed probability inequality.

On a failed threshold event use the deterministic in-band fallbacks stipulated in def:endpoint-learning-handle.  Matrix inversion on the open set above threshold, clipping, finite sums, and parameter-dependent Lebesgue integrals are Borel measurable; the fallbacks therefore make the learner a total measurable sample map.  For large \(M\), the floor in \(J_M\) gives \(h_M\asymp\{\log(M+2)/M\}^{1/12}\), so each of the first two terms in \(r_M\) is of order \((\log M/M)^{1/3}\), and the third is smaller.  This completes the affirmative answer.

added_lemmas.statement: In a dominated differentiable statistical model, if the real parameter \(\theta\) is pathwise differentiable at \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\) with canonical gradient \(D\in L_0^2(P)\), then the limit distribution of every regular estimator is the convolution of \(N(0,E_P[D(O)^2])\) and another probability law.  In particular, whenever its asymptotic variance exists, it is at least \(V_P=E_P[D(O)^2]\).

source.verbatim_statement: Suppose that the sequence of experiments is locally asymptotically normal and that the estimator sequence is regular. Then its limit distribution is the convolution of the efficient normal distribution and another probability distribution.

attestation.note: Transcribed from van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 25.20, and specialized in the node statement to the scalar canonical gradient.

proposed.statement: For every \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\), \(D=D_1-D_0\) is the observed-data canonical gradient of \(\theta\) in the locally unrestricted independent-censoring model, the tangent closure generated by admissible smooth submodels has squared norm \(V_P\), and every regular estimator has asymptotic variance at least \(V_P\); the estimator in thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency attains this bound.
proposed.justification: A Gaussian limit alone is insufficient; this result certifies that the singular endpoint score is the efficiency benchmark and that the feasible procedure attains it.
proposed.gap: Westling et al. (2024), Theorem 2, derives the survival-at-time gradient under positive censoring through the horizon, while the present gradient is the directly integrated fixed-endpoint score on a model with \(G_a(1\mid x)=0\).
proposed.consumer: The efficiency certificate lets applied analysts compare alternative adjusted RMST procedures on the correct endpoint information scale.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof invokes the classical semiparametric convolution bound, so the cited leaf must be declared in the theorem's proof spine.
